items.title: UAE calls for de-escalation after 1,400 Iranian attacks

featured_image.name: UAE envoy to UN urges de-escalation of US-Israeli war with ...

items.description:
The United Arab Emirates on Monday called for an immediate de-escalation of the US-Israeli war with Iran and a return to negotiations, as the Gulf state disclosed it had been subjected to more than 1,400 Iranian drone and missile attacks since the conflict erupted on February 28.

"De-escalation, de-escalation, de-escalation. This is our position and we will continue to offer it," UAE Ambassador Jamal Jama al Musharakh told reporters during a press briefing at the United Nations in Geneva, according to Reuters.[1]

items.title: US intercepts Iran signal that may activate sleeper cells abroad

featured_image.name: Iran may be activating sleeper cells outside the country, alert says

items.description: Nearly two weeks into Operation Epic Fury, the joint US-Israeli air campaign that began on February 28, Iran's decentralized military doctrine is being put to its most severe test — and by several accounts, it is holding. Despite the killing of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and senior military commanders, Iran has continued launching waves of ballistic missiles and drones at targets across the Middle East, raising questions about whether airpower alone can neutralize the Islamic Republic's war-fighting capacity.

items.title: HSBC CEO reaffirms confidence in Gulf amid Iran war

featured_image.name: Incoming HSBC boss Georges Elhedery mulls middle management ...

items.description:
HSBC CEO Georges Elhedery on Monday voiced the bank's continued confidence in the Gulf region's economic prospects, making him one of the first international bank leaders to publicly address the growing crisis as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran enters its second week.

"HSBC remains steadfast in our confidence in the GCC and in the long-term strength, resilience and promise of the region," Elhedery said in a statement, according to Reuters. "We continue to believe that the years ahead will bring renewed stability, growth, and prosperity."[1]

items.title: Iran war produces largest oil supply disruption in history, Rapidan Energy says

featured_image.name: Iran war threatens prolonged hit to global energy markets ...

items.description:
The U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, now in its tenth day, has produced the largest oil supply disruption in recorded history, sending energy prices surging and intensifying calls from analysts and policymakers to accelerate the shift toward renewable energy sources.

Roughly 20% of global crude oil and natural gas supply has been suspended since the conflict began on February 28, according to Reuters, after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz and attacked energy infrastructure across the Persian Gulf. Crude oil prices have climbed above $100 per barrel, with consulting firm Rapidan Energy calling the disruption nearly three times greater than the 1973 Arab oil embargo.[1][2]

items.title: Russia says it is 'not neutral' in US-Iran war

featured_image.name: Russia provided Iran with intelligence on US military ...

items.description: Russia's ambassador to the United Kingdom declared on March 8 that Moscow is "not neutral" in the war between the United States and Israel on one side and Iran on the other, the most explicit public acknowledgment yet of Russia's alignment in a conflict that has reshaped the geopolitics of the Middle East in barely two weeks.

items.title: Iran war splits BRICS as India blocks joint response

featured_image.name: Brics missing in action as war on permanent member Iran ...

items.description:
More than a week into the U.S.-Israeli military campaign against Iran, the BRICS coalition has failed to issue a single collective statement on a conflict engulfing one of its own members — a silence that analysts say lays bare the limits of the 11-nation bloc's ambitions to reshape the global order.

The absence of a unified response stands in contrast to June 2025, when BRICS, then under Brazil's chairmanship, swiftly condemned coordinated U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran as a violation of international law. This time, under India's rotating presidency, the organization has been conspicuously quiet since Operation Epic Fury began on February 28, killing more than 1,230 people in its first six days.[1][2]

items.title: Macron announces naval mission to reopen Strait of Hormuz

featured_image.name: France to deploy almost dozen warships, mulls Hormuz mission ...

items.description:
French President Emmanuel Macron announced Monday that France and its allies are organizing a "purely defensive" naval mission to escort commercial ships through the Strait of Hormuz, the critical waterway that has been effectively shut since the start of the U.S.-Israeli military campaign against Iran on February 28.

Speaking in Cyprus after meeting with Cypriot President Nik Christodides and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, Macron said the escort operation "must be collaboratively prepared with both European and non-European nations" and would aim to progressively reopen the strait, through which roughly 20% of global oil production normally flows.[1][2]

items.title: Greek tanker exits Hormuz with Saudi crude as traffic slowly resumes

featured_image.name: Oil supertanker rates hit all-time high as Iran pledges to close the Strait of Hormuz

items.description:
A Greek-operated oil tanker carrying a million barrels of Saudi crude has become one of the first large vessels to exit the Persian Gulf since the Strait of Hormuz was effectively shut down by Iranian attacks more than a week ago, according to Bloomberg, even as the vast majority of shipping operators remain unwilling to risk the passage.[1]

The Shenlong, operated by Greece's Dynacom Tankers Management Ltd., switched off its transponder in the Persian Gulf on March 4 while heading toward Hormuz and began signaling again off the coast of India on Monday morning, ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg showed. U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright confirmed the transit in a weekend interview with Fox News, and told CNN that a broader resumption of traffic was "not too long away," adding that the worst-case timeline was "a few weeks, that's not months".[2][1]

items.title: G7 fails to agree on oil reserve release as crude tops $100

featured_image.name: G-7 to Discuss Joint Release of Emergency Oil Reserves

items.description:
Finance ministers from the Group of Seven nations held an emergency call Monday morning to discuss the historic surge in oil prices but failed to reach consensus on a joint release of strategic petroleum reserves, with France saying the bloc is "not there yet" on organizing a global drawdown.

French Finance Minister Roland Lescure made the remarks after the virtual meeting, according to Bloomberg, which reported that the G7 is "not there yet" in terms of a coordinated release of emergency oil inventories despite the escalating crisis triggered by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.[1]

items.title: UN chief to argue Iran war bolsters case for renewables

featured_image.name: The clean energy future is within reach," says UN General Secretary Antonio  Guterres, ETEnergyworld

items.description:
As the U.S.-Israeli air campaign against Iran enters its second week, the conflict's disruption to global fossil fuel supplies has intensified a debate over whether the crisis could accelerate the world's transition to renewable energy. With approximately 20% of global crude oil and natural gas supply suspended and oil prices climbing to their highest levels since 2022, energy experts, world leaders, and industry groups are making the case that homegrown clean power is not just a climate imperative but a matter of national security.[1][2]

U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres plans to press that argument on Monday. "The turmoil we are witnessing today in the Middle East makes it evident that we are facing a global energy system largely tied to fossil fuels — where supply is concentrated in a few regions and every conflict risks sending shock waves through the global economy," Guterres said in an email to The Associated Press. "In past oil shocks, countries had little choice but to absorb the pain. Now they have an exit ramp."[3]

items.title: NATO intercepts second Iranian missile in Turkish airspace

featured_image.name: NATO Nuclear Host Intercepts Iranian Ballistic Missile Near Its Borders —  UNITED24 Media

items.description:
NATO air defense systems shot down a second Iranian ballistic missile in Turkish airspace on Monday, the Turkish Ministry of National Defense confirmed, as debris rained down on uninhabited fields in the southeastern province of Gaziantep. The interception, which occurred at approximately 3:00 p.m. local time, marks the second such incident in five days and deepens a crisis that has drawn the Western alliance closer to direct involvement in the widening U.S.-Iran conflict.[1][2]

Hours later, the U.S. State Department ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave the American consulate in Adana, near the strategic Incirlik Air Base, citing safety risks. Americans in southeastern Turkey were "strongly encouraged to depart now," the department said in an updated travel advisory.[3][4]

items.title: Study finds satellite radar warming could cut high-risk bridge counts by a third

featured_image.name: Satellite study reveals which bridges across Earth are at highest risk ...

items.description: A global study of 744 long-span bridges has found that structures in North America face the highest risk of geo-hazard-related damage anywhere on Earth, with many built during a 1960s construction boom now nearing or surpassing their intended lifespans. The research, published this week in Nature Communications, proposes satellite radar imaging as a tool to monitor aging infrastructure and reduce the number of bridges classified as high risk.[1][2]

items.title: Wall Street slides as Iran conflict sparks oil surge

featured_image.name: Stock Markets Today March 9, 2026: Sensex crashed 2346 ...

items.description:
U.S. stock markets opened with steep losses on Monday as crude oil prices surged above $110 per barrel for the first time since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, deepening fears that the widening conflict in the Middle East will choke global energy supplies and tip the economy toward stagflation.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite all fell sharply at the open, extending a punishing stretch that has dragged major indices lower since their January highs. Futures had pointed to losses of roughly 1.5% before the opening bell. The selling followed a brutal week on Wall Street, with the Dow closing Friday at 47,502 after dropping nearly 1% in that session alone.[1][2]

items.title: Trump says ending Iran war will be 'mutual' decision with Netanyahu

featured_image.name: Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu meets with President Trump in Florida

items.description: President Donald Trump said Sunday that the decision to end the war with Iran will be made jointly with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, though he indicated he would retain final authority. The remarks, made in a brief phone interview with The Times of Israel, came as Iran formally named Mojtaba Khamenei as its new supreme leader and fighting across the Middle East entered its tenth day.[1][2]

items.title: Von der Leyen says 'no tears' for Iran regime, drawing EU diplomat backlash

featured_image.name: Ursula von der Leyen to announce bid for second term as head of European  Commission

items.description: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen drew sharp criticism from EU diplomats on Monday after she declined to condemn American and Israeli military strikes on Iran and declared that "there should be no tears shed for the Iranian regime" during a speech at the annual EU Ambassadors Conference in Brussels. The remarks deepened an institutional rift over who speaks for Europe on foreign policy as the 10-day-old war in Iran continues to roil the Middle East.

items.title: NATO shoots down second Iranian missile over Turkey in a week

featured_image.name: Iranian missile heading toward Türkiye downed by NATO ...

items.description:
NATO air defense systems intercepted a second ballistic missile fired from Iran that entered Turkish airspace on Monday, Turkey's Defense Ministry confirmed, marking the second such incident in less than a week and deepening fears that the broader Middle East conflict could draw in the Western alliance.

The interception occurred at approximately 3:00 PM local time, with debris landing in uninhabited areas of Turkey's southeastern Gaziantep province, according to the ministry's statement. No casualties or injuries were reported. Reuters reported that the ministry emphasized it would "act promptly and decisively as needed" and urged all parties to heed Ankara's warnings.[1][2]

items.title: Microsoft launches Copilot Cowork with Anthropic's Claude for enterprise AI agents

featured_image.name: Microsoft adds Anthropic's Claude AI models to 365 Copilot ...

items.description:
Microsoft announced on Sunday a new Copilot Cowork feature built in close collaboration with Anthropic, marking a deepening of the two companies' partnership and the software giant's most aggressive push yet into AI agents for enterprise customers. The feature, part of what Microsoft is calling "Wave 3" of its Microsoft 365 Copilot journey, uses Anthropic's Claude model and the same underlying agentic framework as Anthropic's standalone Claude Cowork product.[1]

Copilot Cowork is designed to handle long-running, multi-step tasks — such as assembling a presentation, pulling together financials, emailing a team, and scheduling prep time — all from a single request. "We really believe right now is an inflection point," Jared Spataro, Microsoft's chief marketing officer for AI at Work, told Fortune. "The inflection point for us is Copilot taking on these agentic capabilities and going from assistance to real doing."[1]

items.title: Asian markets plunge as oil tops $100 amid Iran conflict

featured_image.name: Oil prices top $90 on Iran war

items.description: A sharp spike in crude oil prices past $100 a barrel sent shockwaves through Asian markets on Monday, with Japanese stocks suffering their steepest single-day decline since April and the Indian rupee sliding to an all-time low as the escalating U.S.-Israel military campaign against Iran continued to choke global energy supplies.

items.title: Musk pushes vision of robot-powered 'sustainable abundance'

featured_image.name: Tesla CEO Elon Musk on Optimus robot: This will be the biggest product ever  of any kind

items.description: Elon Musk is doubling down on his vision of a future where artificial intelligence and robots handle all labor, rendering traditional work optional and ushering in an era of what he calls "sustainable abundance." The Tesla CEO's sweeping predictions, repeated across forums from Davos to podcasts in recent months, have drawn both fascination and sharp criticism from economists, politicians, and fellow tech leaders.

items.title: South Korea, Taiwan cap fuel prices as oil tops $100

featured_image.name: Gov't to extend fuel tax cut by another 2 months until April

items.description: South Korea and Taiwan moved on Monday to impose caps on domestic fuel prices as surging oil costs driven by the expanding conflict between the United States, Israel, and Iran ripple through energy-dependent Asian economies.
